title: Thermal Complexity Grows With AI Chips And Photonics
gist: An EDA and design roundtable (Synopsys, Silvaco, Vinci, Keysight, Siemens EDA) argues photonics and multi-die AI packages need transient, multi-physics (thermal, stress, optical, electrical) simulation early in design, hierarchical vendor-supplied models, and aging-aware tools that do not exist yet.

insights.claim: Photonics can cut data-center bottlenecks but cannot scale today because large mesh switches need many components with high losses, requiring a modular scalable architecture, and the thousands of heaters needed for thermal control make calibration hard.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Optical interconnect scaling is gated by loss and control complexity; temper timelines for photonic switch adoption.
insights.quote: Photonics has a lot of promise for reducing data center bottlenecks, but it can’t be scaled right now.
insights.locator: Mueth: Photonics has a lot of promise

insights.claim: Co-packaged optics needs simulation in the transient domain because heat from an ASIC lingers, even a very small temperature change can shift a ring oscillator, and steady-state simulation misses this.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Transient thermal-optical simulation is a gap for CPO viability, creating opportunity for multi-physics EDA vendors.
insights.quote: Even a very small change in temperature can shift the ring oscillator.

insights.claim: Mounting the EIC driver near or on top of the PIC creates heat pollution and stresses that can affect optical signals even more than thermal effects, so moving components can make things worse instead of better.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Stress is a first-order issue in CPO packaging, not just heat; packaging design trade-offs are non-obvious.
insights.quote: Just by moving something, you can make things worse instead of better.

insights.claim: Silicon photonics behaves like analog circuits, with always-on DC current and large signal swings that heat the waveguide interconnect, and the heaters needed to run the EIC must be placed far enough apart to avoid hot spots.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Photonics thermal design differs fundamentally from digital CMOS, so digital-derived tools do not transfer.

insights.claim: Photonic ICs are far more sensitive to warpage and thermal gradients than electronic ICs, potentially tripling the multi-physics, digital-twin and surrogate-model need, and require four solvers (electrical, mechanical, thermal, optical); Silvaco's Berg says this is why photonics has been the next big thing for 30 years.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Skeptical read on photonics timelines; complexity supports tool vendors but delays adoption.
insights.quote: photonics has been the next big thing in the semiconductor world for the past 30 years
insights.locator: Berg: Thermal variation on a PIC chip

themes.theme: Multi-die AI packages and transient design

insights.claim: Thermal, electrical and mechanical modeling must be done up front at architecture time, including high-performance use-case corners; running each solver standalone misses the coupled steady state.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Shift-left multi-physics is the design-flow change that creates demand for integrated simulation platforms.
insights.locator: Mueth: Yes, and when you’re doing the architecture

insights.claim: AI chips are moving from training to inference and stacking dies to increase bandwidth, so the relevant question is transient headroom; for inference a data center could define a design rule such as a millisecond power pulse every 100 milliseconds, a new paradigm to exploit.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Pulsed-power design rules could unlock extra inference performance within thermal budgets; watch for transient-aware power management.
insights.quote: For inference, I can allow a millisecond pulse every 100 milliseconds.
insights.locator: Radhakrishnan: If you look at the direction AI chips

insights.claim: Hierarchical thermal models supplied by each vendor (e.g. HBM makers providing an HBM model to integrators who assemble the multi-die stack) are a must for capacity and for the ecosystem, and need agreed standards so models can be shared.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Model-exchange standards for HBM and chiplets are an unresolved ecosystem gap; standardization progress could favor open-model vendors.
insights.locator: Lin: Going back to the question about hierarchical models

insights.claim: Thermal sensors are increasingly embedded in dies to monitor aging, with software throttling chip regions based on sensor feedback, and this matters especially for automotive chips that must last 10 to 15 years.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Aging-aware runtime management is becoming a design requirement, especially for automotive and data-center parts.
insights.locator: Radhakrishnan: I’m seeing a lot of thermal sensors

insights.claim: Reliability falls substantially for every 10 degrees of temperature rise per the Arrhenius rule of thumb, and ambient conditions such as in Saudi Arabia make this more important to get right.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Hot-climate data centers face reliability penalties, which affects site selection and cooling cost.
insights.locator: Berg: Yes, particularly places like Saudi Arabia

insights.claim: There is a tool gap: the industry lacks accurate prediction of thermally induced aging, and no one has done aging-aware design optimization, which Radhakrishnan calls an under-design/over-design problem that ideally must be dynamic over time.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: White space for EDA vendors to build aging-aware optimization; electromigration risk in data-center data paths is unpriced in design.
insights.quote: I don’t see a lot of tools in the industry for accurately predicting thermally induced aging.
insights.locator: Lin: But I don’t see a lot of tools
